Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Downforce is a card-driven bidding, racing, and betting game for 2-6 players based on Top Race, the award-winning design by the legendary Wolfgang Kramer. Players first bid to own the six cars in the race, then they play cards from their hand to speed them around the track. However, most cards will also move their opponents' cars. So figuring out just the right time to play a card is the key to victory. Along the way, players make secret bets on who they think will win the race. Whoever has the most money (in $ millions) from their prize money, winning bets, and remaining bank, wins. Contents 1 Start of the game 2 Auctions 3 Player's turn 4 End of the game 5 Variants 5.1 Powers 5.2 Betting variants 6 Race Tracks 6.1 River Station and Marina Bay 6.2 Crosstown Speedway 6.3 Switchback Pass 6.4 Aloha Sands 6.5 Savanna Stretch Start of the game The game is composed of: a game board six colored cars (black, blue, green, yellow, orange, red) 42 speed cards with one to six lines with a color and a speed on each six special speed cards with a single speed line power cards with special abilities A race circuit is chosen and all six racing cars are placed randomly on starting spaces. Then, six color cards are shuffled and disposed on a stack. Each player takes an equal number of speed cards (in 4 or 5 player games, 2 cards are not dealt and are left in the box). Auctions The first color card is then drawn and every player will secretly and simultaneously choose a card from their hand to bid on it. The highest speed line matching the current auction color will win the auction and get the car, the special speed card and a power card associated with the car (if this game option has been selected). Winning bids count against your final $M earnings. E.g. if you win the bid with a card listing 5 speed for the current auction, this counts as -$5M at end game. Cards used for bidding are returned to your hand. This means that you may use the same card for different auctions. Wild cards can only be used for a bid if no other cards in hand contain the current auction color. As a last resort, if none of the cards in hand have the current color on auction AND no cards in hand have a wild, then you may play any card for the bid, counting the lowest number as the replacement bid. When all auctions are processed, the race begins. Some notes on auctions for games less than 6 players: All players must win at least 1 car by auction. As such if the remaining number of cars match the remaining number of players, only players who yet to win a car can participate in that auction. Players that win an auction for more than 1 car can only keep 1 of the powers won, if Powers are included in your game . After all auctions end, choose 1 power to keep and discard the rest. All winnings and auction costs for multiple cars are attributed to the the one player. Tie breakers. If more than one player ties for the current auction, the card with more different cars listed wins. If still tied, then the card with fewer Wild symbols shown wins. Rare All Wild/No Bid. There could be a car auction where all players play card bids that either do not correspond to that color, or use a Wild. (Wilds can only be played when no cards in hand have the color being auctioned). In the case of tie in this rare case, this car color is set aside and the rest of the colors are auctioned as planned. [Rating: 1/10] At 6 players, this was one of the worst gaming experiences I've ever had.  The ridiculous range in board states between turns makes any long-term strategic play impossible—as in, you end your turn, and by the time your next turn rolls around, you can have moved anywhere from 0 to 20+ spaces. But the game wants you to *think* you're playing a strategy game by asking you to look at your hand and bid on a car at the start, so it's totally at odds with itself. [Rating: 1/10] After another play I can see some issues with it  it is way too long with a tendency for players to overthink it. You are incentivised to bet on your own car.  There are better gamble/race games out there.

[Rating: 1/10] The betting system means the leaders of the first betting phase are most likely to get bets and pull way ahead... leaving for lame races.  This makes for one of the most disappointing "races" I've ever had the displeasure of experiencing.

[Rating: 1/10] It's like playing two completely different games at once - a betting one, and a racing one. Problem is, I don't particularly like either.

[Rating: 1/10] I've never played a game where the first player can block everyone else from ever getting ahead, and it only got worse as the game progressed.  I'm not one to usually blast a game after a single play but that's insanely bad design.

[Rating: 2/10] This is not so much a racing game, as a brutally painful game of parking in corners. Racers find a constrained curve, stop, get out, have lunch, and literally never move until forced too. It’s ridiculous. It’s hard to overstate how not fun this game was. Race games are hard, but they’re not *this* hard.

[Rating: 2/10] huge runaway leader problem. very little control of anything. who is able to block who is mostly a matter of chance. shared incentives don't function properly. bidding feels like an afterthought. there are many good horse race bidding games that actually accomplish what this is unable to.  i keep trying to give this one a chance, but the more i play it the more it feels like a waste of time. quite possibly the most overhyped game i've ever played.

However, it feels a bit under-baked, probably as cars are 100% owned and as you only have limited betting opportunities and are pretty likely to just bet on whoever is in the lead when you get your second and third betting opportunity, if not your first too.
